A Different Kind of Woman

Spartan women were famous throughout the ancient world for their freedom and physical prowess. Other Greeks found them extraordinary — sometimes admirable, sometimes scandalous. Athenian men wrote about Spartan women with a mixture of fascination and disapproval. Aristotle criticised Sparta for allowing women too much licence, arguing that the power of Spartan women undermined the state. Yet Spartan women themselves would not have understood this criticism: their role was entirely shaped by the needs of the polis, and in fulfilling it they earned genuine respect.

Physical Education and Its Purpose

The most striking feature of Spartan female upbringing was its emphasis on physical fitness. Spartan girls ran, wrestled, threw the discus and javelin, and competed in athletic festivals. This was not for its own sake: the entire educational system in Sparta, for both boys and girls, was designed to serve the state’s military needs. Girls were trained to be physically strong because strong, healthy mothers were more likely to survive childbirth and to produce strong sons for the Spartan army.

This was the fundamental logic of Spartan female education: women existed to serve the state’s need for soldiers. They were not trained to be independent; they were trained to be excellent mothers of warriors. But in practice, the physical freedom this required gave Spartan women a much wider range of experience and confidence than their Athenian counterparts. They moved around in public without restriction, spoke their minds and were accustomed to physical activity in mixed-age groups.

Key Fact

Spartan girls received the same physical training as boys — running, wrestling, javelin, discus — to produce fit mothers of warriors. They could own and inherit property, move freely in public, and were expected to manage estates alone while their husbands were away at war.

Property and Independence

Spartan women had wider property rights than Athenian women. They could own, inherit and manage property in their own right. By the fourth century BC, ancient sources suggest that Spartan women owned approximately two-fifths of Spartan land. This came about partly through accident — the Spartan male citizen population declined dramatically because of warfare losses, leaving estates to female heirs — and partly by design: a Spartan woman needed to be able to manage her husband’s estate when he was absent on campaign or living in the men’s barracks.

This property ownership gave Spartan women a degree of economic independence that was genuinely exceptional in the Greek world. It was also one of the things Aristotle complained about in his Politics. He argued that the wealth of Spartan women made them unwilling to submit to proper discipline, and that their power was a reason for Sparta’s eventual decline. His critique tells us as much about his own Athenian assumptions as it does about Sparta.

Aristotle wrote from an Athenian perspective. In his Politics he argued that the Spartan state had made a fundamental error in neglecting to discipline its women. He saw female freedom as a form of disorder — a state that could not control its women was failing to maintain proper hierarchy. His criticism is useful evidence for how unusual Spartan women appeared to outsiders, but it needs to be used carefully: he was applying Athenian values (female seclusion, male authority) to a society built on entirely different principles. An examiner will reward students who recognise this bias and use it analytically.

The Role of Wife and Mother

The primary role of a Spartan woman was to produce healthy male citizens. Spartan marriage was structured to maximise this. Unlike Athenian men, Spartan husbands did not live with their wives until they were around thirty years old — younger husbands returned to communal quarters after visiting their wives. The syssitia were their dining groups. This arrangement meant that the wife managed the household entirely alone. It also gave her genuine authority within the domestic space: she was the effective head of the household in her husband’s absence.

Spartan women were taught to value courage and patriotism. The famous Spartan sayings about mothers — “come back with your shield or on it” — whether historically accurate or not, reflect a cultural ideal: the Spartan mother who did not weep when her son went to war and who would rather see him die gloriously than return as a coward. Ancient sources collected these sayings and attributed them to Spartan women as evidence of their exceptional patriotism and emotional hardness. The Sayings of Spartan Women, preserved by Plutarch in his Moralia, contains dozens of such remarks.

Key Fact

Spartan husbands continued to return to communal quarters until around age thirty, even after marriage. This meant Spartan wives managed the household and estate alone — giving them real authority in the domestic space, unlike Athenian women who were supervised by their husbands.

Comparison with the Athenian Woman

The contrast between the Athenian and Spartan woman is one of the most productive analytical topics in this unit. Both societies used women primarily to serve the state’s needs — but they defined those needs very differently. Athens needed women to produce legitimate citizen heirs and maintain household stability; this required control and seclusion. Sparta needed women to produce strong warriors; this required physical training and a degree of independence.

The result was two radically different female experiences. The Athenian kyria was defined by her domesticity and invisibility. The Spartan wife was defined by her physical strength, her ability to manage estates alone and her patriotic dedication to the state. Neither was free in a modern sense — both existed to serve male-defined purposes — but within those purposes the Spartan woman had considerably more agency and respect. Material evidence for Spartan women is sparse compared to Athens: there are no Spartan equivalents of the Hegeso Stele, which itself reflects how differently the two cultures memorialised women.

Spartan women had greater physical freedom, property rights and public visibility than Athenian women. They were not secluded; they participated in public athletic festivals; they could manage estates and speak openly. However, it is important not to romanticise their position: they were trained and managed by the state for the state’s purposes. Their freedom was a tool of Sparta’s military system, not an expression of a belief in gender equality. The key analytical move is to recognise that both Athenian and Spartan societies controlled women — they just did so in different ways and for different ends.

A Civilisation Before Classical Greece

When most people think of ancient Greece, they picture the Parthenon, Athenian democracy, and the age of Pericles. But nearly a thousand years before that world existed, a powerful civilisation flourished on the Greek mainland and across the Aegean. The Mycenaean civilisation takes its name from the citadel of Mycenae in the north-eastern Peloponnese, which was its most powerful centre.

The Mycenaean age belongs to what archaeologists call the Late Bronze Age, spanning roughly 1600–1100 BC. At its height, Mycenaean palaces controlled vast territories, organised large-scale agricultural surpluses, and traded across the Mediterranean — with Egypt, the Levant, and the Hittites of Anatolia. Their warriors used bronze weapons and armour, rode horse-drawn chariots, and were buried with extraordinary wealth.

Key Fact

The Mycenaean civilisation flourished from approximately 1600 to 1100 BC. Around 1200–1100 BC, the palace system collapsed. The palaces at Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos were destroyed, probably by a combination of invasion, internal rebellion and climate-related disruption. This collapse plunged Greece into a ‘Dark Age’ of several centuries.

The World Behind Homer

Homer’s Odyssey and Iliad were composed centuries after the Mycenaean age had ended — probably in the 8th century BC. Yet the poems preserve memories of a grander, more heroic age: of great walled citadels, gold-rich kings, bronze-armed warriors, and palaces with grand central halls. Homer calls Mycenae “rich in gold” and describes the palace of Odysseus at Ithaca in terms that match, at least loosely, the archaeological reality of Mycenaean palace life. Scholars debate how much of this detail is historical memory and how much is poetic invention, but the connection between Homer’s world and the Bronze Age is now firmly established.

Scholars are divided about how far Homer reflects real Mycenaean life. Some details in the poems — the use of bronze weapons, the boar’s tusk helmet described in Iliad Book 10, the great feasting halls, the system of gift exchange — do match archaeological finds from the Bronze Age. However, the Odyssey also shows features of the later Iron Age, such as iron tools. This suggests the poems are a layered blend: oral traditions passed down across centuries, gradually incorporating elements of the poet’s own era. The poems are therefore a ‘heroic picture’ — not a documentary record, but not pure fantasy either.

For examiners, the key point is this: the Odyssey and the archaeology of Mycenae illuminate each other, but we must use them carefully. The poems were composed long after the world they describe; the archaeology gives us physical evidence. When both point in the same direction, our confidence grows. When they diverge, we must think carefully about which source to trust — and why.

Heinrich Schliemann and the Excavation of Mycenae

For centuries, the Mycenaean world was known only from myth. It was a German businessman-turned-archaeologist, Heinrich Schliemann, who first brought it to light. Schliemann was convinced that Homer described a real world. He excavated Troy (in modern-day Turkey) in the 1870s and then turned his attention to Mycenae in 1876. His methods were rough by modern standards — he drove trenches directly through layers of archaeological deposit — but the results were extraordinary.

Inside Grave Circle A at Mycenae, Schliemann’s team uncovered six shaft graves filled with spectacular treasures: gold death masks, bronze swords, amber beads, and elaborate jewellery. He was so swept up in the excitement that he famously announced he had “gazed upon the face of Agamemnon” — believing the gold death mask he had found belonged to the legendary king of Mycenae from Homer’s Iliad. In reality, the graves date to around 1550–1500 BC, roughly three hundred years before the traditional date of the Trojan War, so the masks cannot have belonged to Agamemnon. The man buried in Shaft Grave V remains unknown. Nevertheless, the discovery proved that a rich Bronze Age civilisation had indeed existed at Mycenae.

Key Fact

Schliemann excavated Grave Circle A at Mycenae in 1876 and found gold death masks, bronze weapons and rich jewellery in shaft graves. The gold death mask he called the ‘Mask of Agamemnon’ dates to around 1550–1500 BC — too early to have belonged to any historical Agamemnon. Schliemann’s excavations proved Mycenae was a real and wealthy Bronze Age centre, even if his romantic identification with Homer’s heroes was premature.

The Collapse and the Dark Age

Around 1200–1100 BC, the Mycenaean palace system collapsed in a catastrophe that affected much of the eastern Mediterranean. Palaces were burned, Linear B writing disappeared, population levels fell sharply, and trade networks broke down. The cause — or causes — remain debated: archaeologists have proposed invasion by the so-called ‘Sea Peoples’, internal rebellions, earthquakes, drought and famine. Most now favour a combination of stresses rather than a single cause.

Greece then entered a period of reduced complexity often called the Greek Dark Age. Written records disappeared because Linear B — the Mycenaean script — was no longer used. It was not until around 800 BC that the Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and writing returned. It was in this recovering world that Homer’s poems were composed, looking back with nostalgia and wonder at the heroic age that had come before.

The old idea of a single catastrophic invasion no longer convinces most scholars. At Mycenae and Tiryns, fire destruction layers are clear, but the sequence of events at different sites varies. Some palaces show signs of hasty rebuilding; others were abandoned peacefully. Linear B tablets from Pylos suggest that the palace there was preparing for a naval attack shortly before its destruction — but this is unique evidence for one site. The collapse is now seen as a ‘systems collapse’: when interconnected palace economies broke down simultaneously across the eastern Mediterranean, each site fell for locally specific reasons within a wider regional crisis.

Key Mycenaean Sites

The most important Mycenaean sites are Mycenae itself and Tiryns, both in the Argolid region of the Peloponnese, and Pylos in Messenia. Troy (modern-day Hisarlık in north-western Turkey) is also crucial because of its connection to the Homeric tradition. Archaeologists distinguish between Troy VI (destroyed around 1300 BC, probably by an earthquake) and Troy VIIa (destroyed around 1180 BC, possibly in a conflict), and debate which — if either — was Homer’s Troy.
